vulnerabilities.title: UNBOUNDED_STACK_POINTER_NO_BOUNDS_CHECK

root_cause.description: The global postfix evaluation stack pointer 'stack_top' (at 0x4070, initialized to 0x40c0 = start of the 256-element 'stack' array in .bss) is incremented by push() and decremented by pop() with NO bounds checking against the stack array boundaries (lower bound 0x40c0, upper bound 0x48c0). push() writes an 8-byte value at *stack_top then does stack_top += 8 unconditionally. pop() does stack_top -= 8 then reads *stack_top unconditionally. The attacker controls both the number of push/pop operations (via token count and operator placement in the expression string) and the values pushed (via strtoll-parsed 64-bit hex/decimal literals). This allows stack_top to be driven above 0x48c0 (push overflow past stack end) or below 0x40c0 (pop underflow into the FILE* pointer region and GOT region). The underflow direction is especially critical: .bss layout below stack is [0x4080 stdout(8)] [0x4090 stdin(8)] [0x40a0 stderr(8)] [0x40a8 completed.0(1)] [0x40b0 padding] [0x40c0 stack]. Further below .bss is .data (0x4060-0x4078, containing stack_top itself at 0x4070) and .got.plt (0x4000-0x4060, writable due to Partial RELRO). Each operator token causes net -8 to stack_top (pop twice, push once). With ~24 operators from an empty stack, stack_top reaches 0x4000 (GOT.PLT base). A subsequent push of an attacker-specified value writes directly to a GOT entry. The final pop in eval_expr (0x156b) returns the value at the underflowed stack_top to main, which prints it via printf('Result: %lld') — leaking memory contents (FILE* pointers = libc addresses, GOT entries = libc function addresses) as decimal integers.

attack_surface.input: postfix expression string from stdin (max 1023 bytes via read(0, buf, 0x3ff))
data_flow: main: read(0, buf[rbp-0x410], 0x3ff) reads up to 1023 bytes of attacker expression from stdin
main: strips trailing newline, passes buf pointer to eval_expr(buf) via rdi
eval_expr: token-walk loop over expression string; for each char checks is_operator/is_hex_number/is_dec_number/isspace
eval_expr: decimal token -> strtoll(ptr, &ptr, 10) -> push(result) [stack_top += 8, no upper bound check]
eval_expr: hex token (0x prefix) -> strtoll(ptr, &ptr, 0) -> push(result) [stack_top += 8, no upper bound check]
eval_expr: operator token (+,-,*,/) -> pop() [stack_top -= 8, no lower bound check] x2, compute a op b, push(result) [stack_top += 8]
eval_expr: at end of string (0x156b) -> pop() returns value to main
main: printf('Result: %lld', returned_value) prints the popped value to attacker
Net effect: attacker controls stack_top position via push/pop balance and controls values written via push; attacker observes values read via pop through the printed result

security_check.expected: push() must verify stack_top < stack_end (0x48c0) before writing; pop() must verify stack_top > stack_start (0x40c0) before decrementing and reading; eval_expr must track stack depth and reject expressions that would overflow/underflow the 256-element stack
security_check.actual: push() writes *stack_top and increments stack_top += 8 with no comparison against any bound; pop() decrements stack_top -= 8 and reads *stack_top with no comparison against any bound; eval_expr performs no stack depth tracking whatsoever
security_check.missing_or_incorrect: Both upper-bound check (push overflow) and lower-bound check (pop underflow) are entirely missing in push(), pop(), and eval_expr. No bounds check of any kind exists on stack_top.

Each operator = 1 net pop. 24 operators = 48 bytes of input, well within 1023-byte limit.

strtoll returns a full 64-bit long long for both hex (base 0, auto-detects 0x prefix) and decimal (base 10) tokens. The return value is passed directly to push() as rdi. This means the attacker can push arbitrary 64-bit values (e.g., 0xdeadbeef via '0xdeadbeef' token) to any stack_top position, including underflowed positions in the GOT region.

Bidirectional stack_top control: push (via number tokens) moves stack_top +8; operators move stack_top -8 net. Attacker can interleave number tokens and operators to position stack_top at any 8-byte-aligned offset relative to 0x40c0, both above (overflow) and below (underflow). After positioning, a push writes an attacker-controlled 8-byte value at that address. This enables targeted writes to GOT entries, FILE* pointers, or the stack_top pointer itself.

verification_required: Confirm that memory below 0x40c0 (FILE* pointers at 0x4080-0x40a0, GOT at 0x4000-0x4060) is mapped and readable/writable at runtime when pop underflows reach it
Confirm the exact page boundary above 0x48c0 to determine how far push overflow can write before SIGSEGV
Verify that the final pop's returned value is actually printed by printf when stack_top has been underflowed (confirm no intermediate crash prevents reaching the printf)

Verify that operator tokens on an empty stack do not crash before reaching the GOT region (pops read FILE*/GOT values which are valid pointers, arithmetic on them should not fault except potential idiv-by-zero)
Confirm Partial RELRO leaves .got.plt writable at runtime (ELF shows Partial RELRO, GNU_RELRO covers 0x3de8-0x4000 but .got.plt at 0x4000-0x4060 is outside RELRO range)

vulnerabilities.title: DIVISION_BY_ZERO_NO_DIVISOR_CHECK

root_cause.description: The '/' operator handler in eval_expr performs integer division using 'idiv' (signed division instruction at 0x1497) without checking whether the divisor (the second popped value, stored at [rbp-0x18]) is zero. The divisor comes from pop(), which returns either an attacker-pushed value (via strtoll-parsed literal) or an underflowed memory read. If the divisor is zero, the x86-64 idiv instruction raises a SIGFPE (arithmetic exception), terminating the process. The attacker can directly push 0 as a literal (e.g., '0' or '0x0') and then use '/' to trigger this.

attack_surface.input: postfix expression string containing a '/' operator with a zero divisor
data_flow: main: read expression from stdin, pass to eval_expr
eval_expr: attacker pushes 0 (e.g., '0' token -> strtoll returns 0 -> push(0))
eval_expr: '/' operator token -> pop() returns 0 as divisor [rbp-0x18]
eval_expr: at 0x1491-0x1497: mov rax,[rbp-0x10]; cqo; idiv QWORD PTR [rbp-0x18] — divisor is 0 -> SIGFPE

security_check.expected: Before performing idiv, check if the divisor ([rbp-0x18]) is zero and handle the error gracefully (e.g., _abort with 'division by zero' message)
security_check.actual: No zero-check on the divisor before idiv at 0x1497
security_check.missing_or_incorrect: Divisor zero-check is entirely missing. The idiv instruction at 0x1497 executes unconditionally with whatever value pop() returned.

vulnerable_operation.expression: mov rax,[rbp-0x10]; cqo; idiv QWORD PTR [rbp-0x18] — if [rbp-0x18]==0, SIGFPE

impact.reason: The idiv instruction at 0x1497 with a zero divisor raises SIGFPE (arithmetic exception), which by default terminates the process. The attacker can trigger this by sending an expression like '1 0 /' (push 1, push 0, divide). Preconditions: attacker sends a '/' operator when the top-of-stack value (divisor) is zero. This is directly controllable via the '0' literal token.

The SIGFPE crash terminates the calculator process, denying service. The alarm(60) timeout already limits session duration, but the division-by-zero crash provides immediate process termination on attacker demand. Preconditions: same as CRASH — attacker sends expression with zero divisor and '/' operator.

evidence.description: Division operator handler: at 0x1439 cmp eax,0x2f ('/') -> je 0x1491. At 0x1491: mov rax,[rbp-0x10] (dividend); 0x1495: cqo (sign-extend); 0x1497: idiv QWORD PTR [rbp-0x18] (divisor from second pop). No test/cmp/jcc on [rbp-0x18] before idiv. If [rbp-0x18]==0, CPU raises #DE (divide error) -> SIGFPE.

The divisor [rbp-0x18] comes from the first pop() call at 0x141e (pop b). The popped value is either an attacker-pushed literal (e.g., '0' token -> strtoll returns 0 -> push(0)) or an underflowed memory read. In both cases, the value can be zero. The attacker directly controls whether 0 is on the stack via the '0' or '0x0' literal token.

verification_required: Confirm that SIGFPE is not caught by a signal handler (no signal() or sigaction() calls observed in the binary, so default SIGFPE behavior = process termination)
Confirm the expression '1 0 /' triggers the division-by-zero path (divisor = 0 from the '0' token)

non_vulnerabilities.description: read(0, buf, 0x3ff) with buf at [rbp-0x410], stack frame 0x420 bytes. Buffer is 0x410 bytes, read size 0x3ff (1023). No stack buffer overflow: read size (1023) < buffer size (0x410=1040). Canary at [rbp-0x8] protects return address.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: read size is strictly less than buffer allocation. No overflow of the stack buffer in main.

non_vulnerabilities.description: printf('Result: %lld', ret) uses a compile-time constant format string. No format string vulnerability.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: Format string is a string literal in .rodata, not attacker-controlled. printf is called with a fixed format and one argument.

non_vulnerabilities.description: strtoll call sites: hex uses base 0 (auto-detect 0x prefix), decimal uses base 10. endptr is &ptr (local variable at rbp-0x20), correctly advancing the parse pointer past the number. The +1 increment after strtoll skips the separator. Return value is used correctly (pushed to stack).
non_vulnerabilities.reason: strtoll is called with correct base and endptr. The return value (parsed integer) is correctly used. errno is not checked for overflow, but this is a minor robustness issue, not a security vulnerability by itself.

non_vulnerabilities.description: setvbuf(stdin/stdout/stderr, 0, 2, 0) sets unbuffered mode. alarm(60) sets a 60-second timeout. Standard setup, no vulnerability.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: setvbuf mode 2 (_IONBF) is correct for unbuffered I/O. alarm(60) is a standard timeout. No security issue.

non_vulnerabilities.description: read() return value used for newline stripping: if read returns -1 (error), eax-1=-2, cdqe sign-extends to -2, buf[-2] is accessed. This is a theoretical OOB read on error, but read from stdin does not fail under normal conditions.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: read() failure on stdin is not attacker-triggerable under normal operating conditions. The theoretical OOB read at buf[-2] requires read() returning -1, which is a runtime error condition, not an attacker-controlled input scenario. Classified as non-vulnerability due to non-triggerability.

non_vulnerabilities.description: is_operator, is_dec_number, is_hex_number are simple character/prefix checks with no memory safety issues. _abort calls printf and exit(1) — clean termination.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: These helper functions perform only register-level comparisons and return 0/1. No memory operations, no vulnerability.

unresolved.reason: S1 reports Partial RELRO. GNU_RELRO covers 0x3de8-0x4000. .got.plt is at 0x4000-0x4060, which is outside the RELRO region, implying it remains writable. However, whether the loader applies mprotect after relocation is not independently confirmed by S2 static analysis.
unresolved.required_next_step: S3 dynamic verification: check mprotect on .got.plt region at runtime, or attempt a GOT write via the pop-underflow+push technique and observe whether the write persists.

unresolved.description: Exact page boundary above _end (0x48c0) for push overflow
unresolved.reason: .bss ends at 0x48c0. The RW LOAD segment likely rounds up to a page boundary (0x5000). Push overflow writes between 0x48c0 and ~0x4fff should land on mapped RW memory. Beyond 0x5000 is likely unmapped. S1 runtime test showed 300 pushes did not crash, confirming at least some overflow is mapped.
unresolved.required_next_step: S3 dynamic verification: determine exact page boundary via /proc/self/maps or by pushing increasing numbers of values until SIGSEGV.

unresolved.description: Whether pop underflow reads of FILE* pointers produce useful leak values
unresolved.reason: stdout/stdin/stderr at 0x4080/0x4090/0x40a0 hold FILE* COPY relocations pointing to libc's _IO_2_1_stdout_/_IO_2_1_stdin_/_IO_2_1_stderr_ structures. Their decimal representation via printf('Result: %lld') would leak libc addresses. Exact runtime values not captured by S2 static analysis.
unresolved.required_next_step: S3 dynamic verification: send an expression that causes pop underflow to 0x4080/0x4090/0x40a0 and observe the printed 'Result' value to confirm it is a libc address.

unresolved.description: Whether intermediate operator pushes during underflow corrupt GOT entries before the final targeted push
unresolved.reason: During the operator underflow sequence, each operator's push writes the computed result (a op b from two underflowed reads) to stack_top-16. When stack_top-16 falls in the GOT region, GOT entries get overwritten with arithmetic results of adjacent GOT values. This intermediate corruption may cause crashes before the attacker can complete a targeted GOT overwrite.
unresolved.required_next_step: S3 dynamic verification: trace the exact sequence of GOT writes during operator underflow to determine if a clean targeted write is achievable, or if intermediate corruption prevents reaching the target.
